b: An ad exchange is a technology marketplace where publishers' advertising space is sold to buyers through automated auctions, one impression at a time. When a page, app or streaming player has a slot to fill, the exchange asks connected buyers what they would pay, picks a winner under a published set of rules and passes the winning ad back. It exists because direct sales teams could never price and sell billions of daily impressions by hand, and because the ad networks that bought leftover inventory in bulk gave publishers little visibility into what their audiences were worth. Microsoft's 2007 announcement of its AdECN purchase described the model in terms borrowed from finance: "a true ad exchange is the neutral, transparent, automated connection between multiple ad networks."

The process starts in the publisher's stack. A publisher ad server, such as Google Ad Manager, decides whether a slot goes to a campaign sold directly or to programmatic demand. When programmatic demand gets a turn, the request reaches an exchange, either directly from the ad server, through a supply-side platform (SSP) or through header bidding wrappers such as Prebid.

The exchange then builds a bid request. In most of the market this follows OpenRTB (Open Real-Time Bidding), the IAB Tech Lab protocol whose objects describe the impression, the site or app, the device, the user signals available under consent rules and any deals attached. The bid request is posted to connected demand-side platforms (DSPs) and other bidders, which have a fixed timeout to respond. Each response carries a price, usually expressed as a cost per thousand impressions (CPM), plus the creative markup or a pointer to it and, where relevant, a deal ID.

The exchange applies its rules. Bids below the publisher's price floor are discarded, as are bids that break the publisher's blocks on advertiser categories or domains. Among the rest, the highest bid wins. Under a first-price auction, now the norm, the winner pays what it bid. Google moved Ad Manager to a unified first-price model in an announcement of March 6, 2019; before that most exchanges ran second-price auctions, in which the winner paid a small increment above the runner-up. A win notice goes to the successful bidder, the creative renders and the exchange bills the buyer and pays the seller, keeping a share as its fee.
Not every transaction is an open free-for-all. Exchanges carry three broad modes:
Open auction, where any approved buyer can bid.
Private marketplace, an invitation-only auction tied to deal IDs, covered in PPC Land's private marketplace explainer.
Programmatic guaranteed, a fixed-price, fixed-volume deal that uses the exchange's pipes without an auction.

Transparency standards sit around the auction. Publishers list authorised sellers in ads.txt files; exchanges publish their seller accounts in sellers.json; and the SupplyChain object (schain) inside the bid request records each company that handled it.

The fee is the exchange's revenue line. The Virginia federal court found that Google's exchange, AdX, held a take rate near 20% for more than a decade. Index Exchange moved to dynamic pricing in October 2025, varying its take by transaction.

On the sell side, the large operators include Google's AdX (sold to buyers as Authorized Buyers and to publishers inside Google Ad Manager), Magnite, PubMatic, Index Exchange and OpenX. Most began as SSPs or yield managers and now operate their own auctions, so the company and the exchange are usually the same entity. OpenX said it processes 3 million queries per second on its own hardware, an indication of the volume involved. On the buy side, the participants are DSPs, agency trading desks and, increasingly, automated buying agents.

The first exchanges were built for ad networks rather than advertisers. Right Media, founded in New York in 2003, ran the Right Media Exchange. Yahoo took a 20% stake in October 2006 and agreed on April 30, 2007 to buy the rest for about $680 million, according to its filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. At that time, more than 20,000 buyers and sellers traded over four billion impressions a day on the platform, according to the same release. Microsoft followed on July 26, 2007, agreeing to buy AdECN, a Santa Barbara-area exchange founded in 2003 with about 30 staff. "Joining forces with Microsoft will provide the capital and resources to enable AdECN to scale the exchange," said William Urschel, its founder.

DoubleClick had an exchange in development from at least 2007, before Google bought the company, according to Search Engine Land. Google's rebuilt DoubleClick Ad Exchange was announced on September 17, 2009, according to Google's AdWords blog; PPC Land's backfill explainer dates the launch to September 18. It introduced real-time bidding, letting buyers price each impression individually, and dynamic allocation, which let exchange bids compete with a publisher's booked campaigns inside the DART ad server. Google described the product as "a real-time marketplace to buy and sell display advertising space."

Standardisation came next. OpenRTB began as a pilot in November 2010 among three DSPs and three sell-side firms, reached version 2.0 in June 2011 and was adopted by the IAB with version 2.1 in January 2012. Private deals arrived as Google introduced Direct Deals on AdX on September 15, 2011. In June 2018 Google merged DFP and AdX into Google Ad Manager, and the 2019 first-price switch brought unified pricing rules, which stopped publishers from setting a higher floor for AdX than for rivals.

In January 2026 IAB Tech Lab published Programmatic Auction Definitions for comment. The 12-page document defined 12 roles, including a "final auctioneer", and described an auction as "the process an entity receiving competing bids uses to qualify, evaluate, and decide which to pursue and which to ignore."

The exchange is where the price of open-web display inventory is set, so its rules decide how much of an advertiser's budget reaches publishers. Evidence before the US court put AdX at 63% to 71% of open-web display exchange transactions. On April 17, 2025, Judge Leonie Brinkema found that Google had monopolised the publisher ad server and ad exchange markets and unlawfully tied the two. The European Commission reached a parallel finding on September 5, 2025, when it fined Google 2.95 billion euros for favouring AdX since 2014.

For buyers, exchange choice affects reach, fees and data quality. Agency group PMG moved its buying inside Index Exchange to reach 3,000 media owners, a sign that buyers now deal with exchanges directly rather than only through DSPs.

The central dispute concerns conflicts of interest. When one company runs the publisher's ad server, the exchange and buying tools, it can route demand to itself. The US court examined first look, which gave AdX early access to impressions, and last look, which let it bid after seeing rivals' prices. Teads sued Google on August 3, 2026, claiming rival exchanges lost 6.88 trillion impressions between 2017 and 2023 because Google Ads demand flowed almost entirely through AdX. Google argues its integration improves ad safety and yield.

Fees are a second fault line. Exchanges acting as principals can keep a spread between buying and selling prices. Guardian News and Media sued Rubicon Project on March 31, 2017, over buyer-side fees layered on a 10% seller fee; Rubicon dropped buy-side fees that November. A December 2023 study by the Association of National Advertisers (ANA) found that 36% of post-transaction programmatic budget reached valid, viewable, measurable impressions.
Privacy is the third. Bid requests broadcast device and location signals to many bidders, most of whom lose and keep the data. Google has faced a security complaint over real-time bidding data.

Supply-side platform: software that manages a publisher's sales to automated buyers, with floors, deal management and reporting. PPC Land's SSP explainer describes the exchange as "the marketplace where auctions clear." Most SSPs now run exchanges, which blurs the line.
Ad network: an intermediary that buys or aggregates inventory and resells it, often in packages and at a margin, rather than running an impression-level auction open to many buyers.
Demand-side platform: the buyer's bidding tool. A DSP submits bids into exchanges; it does not hold the auction.
Ad server: the system that decides which ad fills a slot across all sales channels; the exchange is one source of demand it calls.
Unrelated products share the word, including Microsoft's Exchange Online email service and Salesforce's AgentExchange marketplace.

On September 2, 2026, Judge Brinkema refused to order a sale of AdX, writing that "structural remedies are neither realistic nor needed." The 106-page opinion, unsealed on September 16, requires Google to make AdX bids available to rival ad servers and to Prebid on functionally equivalent terms, bans first look and last look, and appoints a technical monitor for six years. The parties filed a joint proposed final judgment on October 2, 2026, with disputed deadlines: six months for the Prebid integration in the plaintiffs' version, twelve in Google's. As of November 28, 2026, entry of a final judgment had not been confirmed in the sources reviewed.

Prebid has proposed reversing the auction order, so that Google Ad Manager submits its offers into a Prebid-run final auction. Analyst Karsten Weide estimates broad adoption in 2028 or later. On November 18, 2026, IAB Tech Lab published OpenRTB 2.6-202611, which moves the SupplyChain object to version 1.1 and extends disclosure to every entity that took custody of a bid request, not only those in the payment flow.

Who: Exchange operators such as Google (AdX), Magnite, PubMatic, Index Exchange and OpenX; publishers and their ad servers on the sell side; DSPs, agencies and buying agents on the buy side; regulators and courts in the US and EU.
What: A marketplace that auctions individual ad impressions in real time, applying floors, blocks and deal rules, and taking a fee on each transaction.

When: Early exchanges appeared from 2003, with Right Media and AdECN acquired in 2007; Google's AdX with real-time bidding arrived in September 2009; OpenRTB was standardised in 2011-2012; US conduct remedies were ordered on September 2, 2026.
Where: Across websites, mobile apps, connected TV and digital out-of-home screens worldwide, sitting between the publisher's ad server and buyers' DSPs.

Why: Impression-level auctions let publishers price inventory against many buyers at once and let advertisers buy specific audiences at scale, while the concentration of exchange, ad server and buying tools in single companies has made exchanges the focus of antitrust cases.
